howItWorks.intro: Each of the five inputs below is scored on its own step scale (in points, not straight percentages) and then summed into your total out of 100 — here's exactly where the numbers come from:
howItWorks.outro: These breakpoints come from occupational-health and sleep research, not a personal diagnosis — someone who's built a life around 45 work hours and thin social time might genuinely feel fine, and someone hitting every threshold might still feel stretched thin. Treat a low score as a prompt to look at the specific factor dragging it down, not as a verdict on how you're doing.

faq.question: What counts as a good work-life balance score here?
faq.answer: On this calculator, 80+ earns an 'A — Excellent Balance,' 65-79 a 'B,' 50-64 a 'C — Needs Attention,' 35-49 a 'D — At Risk,' and under 35 an 'F — Burnout Risk.' In practice, an A usually needs roughly a 40-hour work week, exercise most days, at least 7.5 hours of sleep, real social or hobby time, and most vacation days actually used. Missing badly on just one factor — chronic short sleep is the most common culprit — is enough to pull an otherwise strong week down to a B or C.

faq.question: How many hours a week is too many to work?
faq.answer: The scoring gives full marks at 40 hours or fewer and drops 5 points at each 5-hour step past that, bottoming out above 55. That mirrors a 2021 WHO/ILO analysis finding people who work 55+ hours a week face roughly 35% higher stroke risk and 17% higher risk of dying from ischemic heart disease than those working 35-40 hours — the breakpoints follow where the health data shows risk actually climbing, not round numbers chosen for convenience.

faq.question: Why does my score jump so much from changing just one field?
faq.answer: Because the five factors carry different maximums: work hours and exercise can each swing your total by up to 25 points, sleep and social time by up to 20, vacation by only 10. Moving sleep from under 6 hours to 7.5+ is worth 15 points on its own; moving vacation from under 5 days to 15+ is worth at most 8. Two changes that feel equally significant in real life aren't scored equally — the weighting follows how strongly each factor tracks with health outcomes in the research, not how it feels day to day.

faq.question: My score is high but I still feel burned out — what's going on?
faq.answer: The five inputs here are weekly averages; they can't see commute time, caregiving load, how emotionally draining the work itself is, or stress carried over from a rough quarter. A high score means your logged habits look sustainable on paper. If you still feel depleted despite that, the gap is real information — it usually points at something outside these five fields, and it's worth raising with a doctor or therapist rather than something a calculator can resolve.

faq.question: How exactly is the balance score calculated?
faq.answer: Work hours, exercise days, social/hobby hours, and sleep hours are each scored on a step scale — sleep, for example, earns 20 points at 7.5+ hours, 15 at 7, 10 at 6, and 5 below that. Vacation days used this year score on a four-step scale worth 2, 5, 8, or 10 points. The five scores are summed for a total out of 100, and the category contributing the smallest share of its own maximum is named as your top area to improve. Everything runs in your browser — nothing you enter is sent to a server.

howWeCalculate.intro: The calculator scores your five inputs independently against fixed point scales (see the breakdown above), adds them for a total out of 100, and separately identifies whichever category contributes the smallest share of its own maximum as your 'top area to improve' — usually more actionable than the total score alone.
steps: Enter a typical week's hours, not your busiest one — if hours swing widely, average your last three or four weeks before typing a number in
Add exercise days, social or hobby hours, and average nightly sleep, rounded to the nearest half hour — the sleep scale steps at 6, 7, and 7.5 hours, so half-hour precision changes the score
Enter vacation days actually taken so far this year, not days accrued or approved — unused time off doesn't score any points
The score, letter grade, and top-issue callout appear instantly and recalculate live if you change any field afterward
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: The point scales are built from general findings in occupational-health, sleep, and time-use research (including WHO/ILO working-hours data) and describe population-level patterns, not your individual risk. They're a starting point for reflection, not a clinical assessment — a doctor or therapist is the right resource for anything the score raises real concern about.

whenToUse.intro: Run this when something about your schedule is changing or about to change, or when a check-in is overdue — the score means more as a comparison across time than as a single snapshot.
scenarios: Before accepting a new role, promotion, or schedule change, using the hours it would realistically require to see how your score would move
During a performance-review cycle, when work hours tend to creep up gradually without anyone noticing week to week
Right after a change like a new commute, a shift change, or a return-to-office mandate, to check whether it quietly ate into sleep or social time
As a monthly or quarterly check-in, since a single week's numbers are noisy but a trend across several months isn't
When you feel burned out but can't pinpoint why — the top-area flag usually names the habit that slipped first, even if it wasn't the one you suspected

sections.title: What Is the Work-Life Balance Calculator?
sections.body: This calculator turns five weekly habits — hours worked, days exercised, hours spent on hobbies or people outside work, average nightly sleep, and vacation days taken this year — into a single 0-100 balance score, a letter grade from A to F, and a named 'top area to improve.' Work hours are scored on a five-step scale: 25 points at 40 hours or fewer, then 20, 15, 10, and finally 5 points once you cross 55, breakpoints that roughly track where occupational-health research starts flagging elevated risk rather than round numbers chosen for looks. Exercise, social time, sleep, and vacation each follow their own step scale with different ceilings (25, 20, 20, and 10 points), so the five factors aren't weighted equally — sleep and exercise alone can account for 45 of the 100 possible points, more than work hours and vacation combined. The five scores are added for your total, and whichever category scored lowest relative to its own maximum gets named as the habit worth fixing first.

sections.title: Why This Calculation Matters
sections.body: A week is 168 hours, full stop, which is why this scores weekly totals rather than any single day — a 12-hour Tuesday balanced by a light Friday isn't a problem; the same 11-hour day repeated across all fifty-two weeks of a year is, even though no individual day looks extreme on its own. Take a schedule a lot of salaried employees would call unremarkable: 50 hours of work, 2 exercise days, 5 hours of social or hobby time, 6 hours of sleep a night, and 5 vacation days used this year. Run those through the calculator's actual point scale and you get 15 (work) + 15 (exercise) + 15 (social) + 10 (sleep) + 5 (vacation) = 60 out of 100 — a 'C — Needs Attention,' with vacation flagged as the top issue since its 5 points sit furthest below its own 10-point ceiling. Fix exactly that flagged issue — take 15 vacation days instead of 5 — and the total rises to 65, crossing into 'B — Good Balance' on that single change. Compare that to what fixing sleep instead would have been worth: moving from 6 hours a night to 7.5+ is worth a full 10 points (10 to 20), twice the 5-point gain from the vacation fix, which tracks sleep-deprivation research showing six hours a night produces measurable next-day cognitive impairment that extra vacation days don't offset. Push every input to its ceiling — 40 hours of work, 4+ exercise days, 10+ social hours, 7.5+ hours of sleep, 15+ vacation days — and the same formula tops out at a perfect 100. One limitation worth knowing: these five inputs don't include commute time. A one-hour commute each way quietly consumes 10 hours a week that never appear anywhere in this calculator, yet time-use research consistently ranks commute length among the strongest predictors of how balanced people say they feel — worth weighing mentally even though the score can't see it.

sections.title: When Should You Use This Calculator?
sections.body: This is most useful as a recurring check-in rather than a one-time verdict — a single week's numbers are noisy, but a trend across a few months tells you whether a new role, a promotion, or a return-to-office mandate is actually reshaping your time. It's also worth running before you negotiate a job offer or a schedule change: plug in the hours the new arrangement would realistically require and see how the grade shifts before you sign anything. And it's a useful diagnostic mid-burnout — if your score keeps landing in the 40s or 50s despite feeling like nothing dramatic changed, the 'top area to improve' flag usually points at the one habit, often sleep or exercise, that quietly eroded first.

howToSteps.title: Log Your Actual Weekly Work Hours
howToSteps.description: Enter hours actually worked last week, including unpaid overtime and after-hours email — this single input can account for up to 25 of the 100 points, the largest share of any factor.

howToSteps.title: Add Exercise, Social Time, and Sleep
howToSteps.description: Fill in exercise days, hours spent on hobbies or people outside of work, and your average nightly sleep. Together these three fields can contribute up to 65 of the 100 points — more than work hours and vacation combined.

howToSteps.title: Enter Vacation Days Taken So Far This Year
howToSteps.description: Count days actually taken, year to date, not days accrued or approved. If it's mid-year, prorate roughly — 6 days used by August is on pace for about 10-12 by December, which is where the scoring starts rewarding more points.

howToSteps.title: Read Your Score, Grade, and Top Issue
howToSteps.description: Your total out of 100, letter grade, and the single category dragging your score down the most appear instantly. Fixing that one flagged category usually moves your grade more than making small changes across all five fields at once.

tips: Enter a typical week rather than your best or worst one — averaging your last three or four weeks of work hours and sleep produces a more honest score than picking whichever week comes to mind first.
Sleep and exercise together can contribute up to 45 of the 100 points, more than work hours and vacation combined — if your score is low, check those two fields before anything else.
The vacation score only counts days actually taken this year, not accrued PTO — banked time off that never gets used scores zero benefit here, same as it does in real life.

Recalculate after any real change (new job, new commute, a new baby, a schedule shift) rather than trusting an old score — the factor dragging you down six months ago often isn't the one dragging you down now.
If your grade surprises you, look at which single field is closest to its floor rather than staring at the total — the calculator names that field directly as your top area to improve.
